newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish deal with Stasi not illegal - prosecutor.
newsitem.headline: Polish deal with Stasi not illegal - prosecutor.

text.p: Polish prosecutors said on Friday a former communist interior minister who allowed former East Germany's Stasi security police to operate and recruit informers in Poland had not broken the law.

"Former Interior Ministry chief Czeslaw Kiszczak did not break the law when he concluded an agreement in the 1980s allowing the Stasi to operate on Polish soil," Ryszard Kucinski, spokesman for the prosecutor's office, told PAP news agency.
The prosecutors' ruling, which is not subject to appeal, was prompted by a complaint by rightist opposition leader Jan Olszewski.
Olszewski, a dissident lawyer before the 1989 fall of communism, claimed the deal was illegal.

Kiszczak signed an agreement in 1982 allowing the East German Ministry for State Security, or Stasi, and Polish security to operate in each other's countries. The deal came a year after Poland's communist rulers imposed martial law to crush the Solidarity trade union movement.
The Stasi feared that Polish authorities needed help to to stem the democratic protest, which threatened to spill over into East Germany and other communist states.
Kucinski said his office had passed to military authorities, who investigate espionage cases, information on civilians alleged to have informed for the Stasi.
Seven names, who allegedly formed part of a Stasi cell in the Polish capital, had been given to the Solidarity union by a German body investigating the now defunct Stasi, he said.
"The fact that there was an agreement between the services of both countries doesn't alter the fact that someone collaborating with foreign intelligence breaks the law," Kucinski told PAP.
But if Poles recruited by the Stasi had been given approval by the Polish SB they would not have broken the law, he said. It was not however clear if this was the case, he added.
A Warsaw court acquitted Kiszczak in Jyly of charges that a coded message he sent at the outset of martial law in December, 1981, led to police shooting at protesting miners, killing nine.
Former Polish communists, now social democrats, won power as the dominant party in a leftist coalition in 1993.

The ex-communists say abuses committed under communist rule should be prosecuted, but Olszewski and other opposition politicians claim that authorities are failing to act on some cases dating back to the 1970s and 1980s.
